Fun facts:

  • C is not “just a subset of C++”

  • C++ is not “just C with classes”

The differences are important.
C++ is a superset of C. You can write decent programs which will compile with both gcc and g++. It's not just C with classes, but you can write C with classes in C++.

(Comparing here C90 with C++ (03/11/14/17/20/22, take your pick).)

Standard example:

int main()
{
 const int i;
 
 return 0;
}

Compiles as C, doees not compile as C++.

$ g++ C_C++.c
C_C++.c: In function 'int main()':
C_C++.c:3:13: error: uninitialized const 'i' [-fpermissive]
 const int i;
 ^
$ gcc C_C++.c

$

In terms of "compilation", C++ is not a superset of C. Some other examples:

  • enums behaves differently too (even without enum class in C++).
  • C permits pointer type coercions that C++ does not. (C is actually more weakly typed than C++.)
  • Character literals have different sizes on system where char and int have different sizes (so sizeof behaves differently in C and C++)
  • Nested type decls have enclosing-type scope in C, not in C++. (This can cause a name-redefintiion error in C where it does not occur in C++.)

There are others.

In terms of "linking", C has external linkage by default, where C++ has internal (static) linkage by default. (This mostly informs "design" and "architecture, not language semantics, so it's arguably a "soft" point.)
